Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

PETITIONER, RESPONDENT, AND INCIDENT DESCRIPTION
I, Jordan Lee, declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the following is true and correct. I am the petitioner in this matter. The respondent is Pat Morgan. On or about August 15, 2026, at or near 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA, the following occurred: On March 3, 2026, the respondent appeared outside the petitioner’s home and yelled threats for several minutes before leaving. Additional incidents, if any: On March 10, 2026, the respondent sent several threatening text messages to the petitioner. This declaration describes conduct alleged by the petitioner in connection with a request for a civil harassment restraining order under California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "HARASSMENT"
California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(b)(3) defines "harassment," for purposes of a civil harassment restraining order, as unlawful violence, a credible threat of violence, or a knowing and willful course of conduct directed at a specific person that seriously alarms, annoys, or harasses the person, and that serves no legitimate purpose. The course of conduct must be that which would cause a reasonable person to suffer substantial emotional distress, and must actually cause substantial emotional distress to the petitioner.

The course of conduct must be that which would cause a reasonable person to suffer substantial emotional distress, and must actually cause substantial emotional distress to the petitioner."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 527.6(b)(3), the four-part statutory definition of harassment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=527.6)

"COURSE OF CONDUCT" DEFINED
California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(b)(1) defines "course of conduct" as a pattern of conduct composed of a series of acts over a period of time, however short, evidencing a continuity of purpose, including following or stalking an individual, making harassing telephone calls to an individual, or sending harassing correspondence to an individual by any means. Constitutionally protected activity is excluded from the definition.

Constitutionally protected activity is not included within the meaning of "course of conduct.""

TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDER MECHANISM AND HEARING DEADLINE
Under California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6, a petitioner may obtain a temporary restraining order with or without notice to the responding party, based on a declaration showing reasonable proof of harassment and that great or irreparable harm would result absent an order. A request for a TRO without notice is granted or denied the same day it is submitted (or the next judicial business day, if filed too late for review). A TRO issued under this section remains in effect for no more than 21 days, or up to 25 days if the hearing date is extended for good cause, and a full hearing on the petition must be held within that same 21-or-25-day period.

A temporary restraining order may be issued with or without notice, based on a declaration that, to the satisfaction of the court, shows reasonable proof of harassment of the petitioner by the respondent, and that great or irreparable harm would result to the petitioner. (e) A request for the issuance of a temporary restraining order without notice under this section shall be granted or denied on the same day that the petition is submitted to the court... (f) A temporary restraining order issued under this section shall remain in effect, at the court's discretion, for a period not to exceed 21 days, or, if the court extends the time for hearing under subdivision (g), not to exceed 25 days, unless otherwise modified or terminated by the court. (g) Within 21 days, or, if good cause appears to the court, 25 days from the date that a petition for a temporary order is granted or denied, a hearing shall be held on the petition."

WHAT A CIVIL HARASSMENT RESTRAINING ORDER MAY INCLUDE
California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(b)(6)(A) authorizes an order enjoining a party from harassing, intimidating, molesting, attacking, striking, stalking, threatening, contacting (directly or indirectly), or disturbing the peace of the petitioner, and from coming within a specified distance of the petitioner. Section 527.6(c) permits the court, on a showing of good cause, to extend an order to cover other named family or household members.

(c) In the discretion of the court, on a showing of good cause, a temporary restraining order or order after hearing issued under this section may include other named family or household members."

CATEGORIES OF RELIEF AUTHORIZED UNDER § 527.6
The following categories of relief are authorized under California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(b)(6)(A) and section 527.6(c): (1) a personal conduct order that Pat Morgan not harass, intimidate, molest, attack, strike, stalk, threaten, batter, telephone, or contact Jordan Lee, directly or indirectly; (2) a stay-away order that Pat Morgan remain a specified distance from Jordan Lee, with the specific distance and any specified locations set by the order; (3) an order addressing an animal owned, possessed, or kept by Jordan Lee, where applicable under section 527.6(b)(6)(A); and (4) inclusion of other named family or household members, on a showing of good cause under section 527.6(c). Which of these categories to request, and how to complete the corresponding portions of a court petition, is a decision left to the person preparing that petition.

DURATION AND RENEWAL OF A PERMANENT ORDER
California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(j)(1) allows an order issued after notice and hearing to last no more than five years, and permits one renewal, on request, for no more than five additional years without a showing of any further harassment since the original order issued. Section 527.6(j)(2) provides that if the order's expiration date is not stated on the form, the order's duration defaults to three years from issuance.

CRIMINAL CONSEQUENCES OF VIOLATING AN ORDER
California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(t) states that willful disobedience of a temporary restraining order or order after hearing granted under section 527.6 is punishable pursuant to Penal Code section 273.6. Penal Code section 273.6(a) makes an intentional and knowing violation of such an order a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not more than $1,000, imprisonment in county jail for not more than one year, or both. Section 273.6(b) increases the penalty where the violation results in physical injury: a fine of not more than $2,000, imprisonment in county jail for not less than 30 days nor more than one year, or both — though the court may, in the interest of justice and for stated reasons, reduce or eliminate the 30-day minimum if the person has served at least 48 hours.

However, if the person is imprisoned in a county jail for at least 48 hours, the court may, in the interest of justice and for reasons stated on the record, reduce or eliminate the 30-day minimum imprisonment required by this subdivision."

DISTINCTION FROM THE DOMESTIC VIOLENCE PREVENTION ACT
California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(w) states that section 527.6 does not apply to any action or proceeding covered by Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code — California's Domestic Violence Prevention Act. Family Code section 6211 defines "domestic violence" as abuse committed against a spouse or former spouse, a cohabitant or former cohabitant, a person the respondent is or has been dating or engaged to, a co-parent, a child of a party, or a relative within the second degree.

(c) A person with whom the respondent is having or has had a dating or engagement relationship. (d) A person with whom the respondent has had a child... (e) A child of a party or a child who is the subject of an action under the Uniform Parentage Act... (f) Any other person related by consanguinity or affinity within the second degree."

Both statutes are provisions of California law; which category of order applies, and whether an equivalent distinction exists, varies by state.

(e) A child of a party or a child who is the subject of an action under the Uniform Parentage Act... (f) Any other person related by consanguinity or affinity within the second degree.

expectedJSON.gap: California Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(w) expressly states that section 527.6 does not apply to actions or proceedings covered by Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code — California's Domestic Violence Prevention Act (DVPA). Family Code section 6211 defines "domestic violence" by reference to specific relationships between the parties (spouse or former spouse; cohabitant or former cohabitant; a person the respondent is or was dating or engaged to; a co-parent; a child of a party; or a relative within the second degree). A civil harassment restraining order under Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6 and a domestic violence restraining order under Family Code section 6200 et seq. are governed by different statutes, use different Judicial Council forms, and involve different eligibility relationships between petitioner and respondent; a request that in fact involves one of the Family Code section 6211 relationships falls outside what section 527.6 covers. This document addresses only the Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6 civil harassment process and does not cover Domestic Violence Prevention Act proceedings. Both statutes are provisions of California law; which category of order applies, and whether an equivalent distinction exists, varies by state.
